applicationInfo.name: 3D builder for AWS CDK Blocks (sample)
applicationInfo.description:
Threat model version: 6

### What we're working on

This repository is sample code: a 3D builder for AWS CDK Blocks, with the on-screen name Baseplate. A visitor places Blocks on a plate in the browser and sees the AWS resources each one creates. The builder itself runs in the browser from bundled data. The backend adds an agent that picks pieces, saved builds with share links, a live gallery and a here-now count.

A person who clones the repository deploys it into their own AWS account. AWS hosts no running copy. The sample isn't meant for production use.

### Scope

In scope: the code on this branch, the stack it synthesizes (155 resources), and what a stranger inherits by deploying it or copying from it. Out of scope: the deployer's account settings outside the stack (CloudTrail, budgets, other workloads), and the insides of the CDK Blocks library beyond what the stack shows.

### How to read this file

The method is the four questions of the AWS workshop "Threat modeling for builders". Each threat is written in the threat grammar and tagged with its trust boundary, STRIDE letters and a priority. Each mitigation carries `custom:state`, `custom:evidence` (file and line in this repository, or what the synthesized template shows) and `custom:tests` (the test that holds it and the command that runs it).

A mitigation that was seen working on AWS also carries `custom:observed`. An entry that cites `live-deploy/v1/REPORT.md` is from CDK Blocks 1.0.0 (commit `6d13623`, deployed twice and destroyed once on 2026-11-21). Every other entry is from before the move to 1.0.0, when the app ran on `@aws-blocks/blocks` 0.9.0. Those earlier entries cite the maintainers' records of test deploys: `deploy-test/REPORT.md` (the public copy, cloned fresh, deployed to a new stack and destroyed on 2026-11-19) and `live-deploy/REPORT.md`, `live-deploy/REPORT-2.md` and `live-deploy/REPORT-3.md` (this branch deployed over a standing stack on 2026-11-19 and 2026-11-20). The records are kept outside this repository.

Every mitigation has the status Identified and every threat is open. That's deliberate. The method this file follows lets a mitigation be marked resolved only when it rests on behavior ids from a registry with a passing test for each id. This repository has no such registry, and this file doesn't invent ids that nothing checks. The evidence is real and is listed; each open threat's residual risk is for a person to accept, with an owner and an end date, and the approval of a version records those acceptances.

Statements about deployed behavior come from the code, the local tests and a `cdk synth` on 2026-11-27 with the pinned packages (aws-cdk-blocks 1.0.1), except where `custom:observed` cites a test deploy of the earlier release. Not seen on AWS: a throttled request, an alarm firing, the stale-address retry, the opt-in WAF, the retain option, and any Region but us-east-1. The CI workflow has never run.

### Changes since version 5

Version 5 was approved on 2026-11-22. Threats 1 to 23 and mitigations 1 to 29 keep their numbers and ids. No threat or mitigation was added, closed or removed, and no residual risk reads differently except threat 17's.

- Threat 17: aws-cdk-blocks and @aws-cdk-blocks/core moved from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1, four days after their release. The residual risk names that as a third upgrade that didn't wait out the 7-day cooldown, and says what differs between the two releases. The other CDK Blocks packages stay at 1.0.0, which is still their latest release.
- Every statement read from the synthesized template cites a synth of 2026-11-27 with aws-cdk-blocks 1.0.1. The template has the same 155 resources, the same IAM policy text and the same properties as the 1.0.0 synth; only asset hashes, the page build id and the version string differ.
- The README became a short product page. The deploy, cost, teardown and security text it held moved, with its wording kept, to docs/deploy.md, docs/costs.md, docs/teardown.md and docs/security.md. Every evidence entry, mitigation and residual-risk note that cited the README for that text now cites those pages.
- Every file and line reference was located again at this commit.

### Known findings that stay

| Finding | Reason | Look again | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| cdk-nag AwsSolutions, 16 rules in the report of 2026-11-21, report only | npm run nag prints them and isn't a gate. Nearly all sit on resources the CDK Blocks constructs create: wildcard IAM statements, managed policies, no WAF, no API access logs, no authorizer, Lambda defaults, TLSv1 on the default certificate, no secret rotation on either secret. | Each CDK Blocks upgrade | cdk-blocks/scripts/cdk-nag.ts |
| Six of the seven buckets are encrypted with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3), which scanners report as no customer-managed key | Accepted for this sample by the maintainer on 2026-11-21: SSE-S3 is fine here. The buckets hold the built page, logs, the config file and agent session snapshots. The gallery bucket has a customer-managed key through the custom Block. These are CDK Blocks and Hosting defaults. | None set | threat 13, mitigation 17 |
| F10, a stored file with no audit entry | The custom Block's source is generator output. The fix belongs in the generator. | None set | threat 15 |
| F12, presence can be inflated | A fix needs an identity for each client. | None set | threat 16 |
| F13, in part: the always-on render loop and the renderer fallback | Changing the loop alters every animation, and no browser on hand fails the way the fallback needs. | None set | threat 21 |
| F15, in part: no Content-Security-Policy header and no API access logs | Both are CDK Blocks defaults. Access logging changes an account-wide API Gateway role. | None set | threats 14 and 20 |

### Cost exposure for a deployer

These are estimates from list prices for US East (N. Virginia) on 2026-11-19. Nobody has measured them on a bill.

| Case | Estimate | How it was derived |
|---|---|---|
| Idle stack | about 6 to 10 US dollars a month | Counted from the template: 2 KMS keys at $1.00, 1 dashboard at $3.00, 3 alarms at $0.10, 2 secrets at $0.40, plus the once-a-minute job (43,200 runs a month of a 2,048 MB function, assumed at half a second each) and small DynamoDB, S3 and log charges, each put at under $1. |
| Agent at its daily cap | about 0.60 US dollars a day | The caps bound it: 200 questions x 4 model calls x 1,000 output tokens is at most 800,000 output tokens a day, and at the 2,400 input tokens a call that test calls used, about 1.9 million input tokens. Claude Haiku 5.5 through the global inference profile costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts of up to 100,000 tokens (AWS Price List for Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1, published and read 2026-11-20). That's about $0.19 plus $0.40. AgentCore runtime time isn't in it. |
| Flood at the throttle | 10 to 15 US dollars a day | 25 requests a second for 86,400 seconds is 2.16 million requests: about $7.56 for API Gateway at $3.50 per million, $0.43 for Lambda requests, about $3.60 for Lambda time if each request takes 50 ms at 2,048 MB (an assumption), and about $2 for DynamoDB reads. |

### Did we do a good enough job

Every threat links to at least one mitigation, and every mitigation names its evidence. 7 of the 29 mitigations have no test in the repository; each one's `custom:tests` says so. For each mitigation the modeler asked how it could be bypassed, and the answer is in the threat's `custom:residual`. The two threats with the most left to do are the shared throttle (threat 4) and the wide role (threat 12). A version counts once a person has reviewed and approved it.

architecture.description:
### Components

- **Page**: a React 19 and React Three Fiber single-page app, built by Vite and served from a private S3 bucket through CloudFront (the Hosting construct). CloudFront also forwards `/cdk-blocks/api`, the other paths under `/cdk-blocks/` that CDK Blocks reserves, and the earlier prefix `/aws-blocks/*` to the API.
- **API**: one API Gateway REST API with no authorizer, in front of one Lambda function (Node.js 24, 2,048 MB). Every API method is the same route, `POST /cdk-blocks/api`, dispatched by name; `/aws-blocks/api` is an alias that CDK Blocks 1.0 keeps. The function also answers three built-in GET routes of CDK Blocks, `/cdk-blocks/dashboard`, `/cdk-blocks/resources` and `/cdk-blocks/settings`, each with a redirect to the AWS console. Open methods: `getApp`, `joinGallery`, `listGallery`, `getBuild`, `heartbeat`, `checkInvite`, `getProposal`. Methods that need the invite code: `saveBuild`, `agentCreateConversationId`, `agentGetChannel`, `agentStream`, `agentGetConversation`.
- **Realtime**: one API Gateway WebSocket API (the Realtime block) for the gallery channel and the agent's streaming channels.
- **Agent**: the Agent block, running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and calling Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 through its global inference profile, `global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5`. The model thinks before it answers; the thinking counts toward each call's output cap and isn't shown on the page. Its three tools are `browseCatalog`, `snapPieces` and a local stand-in.
- **Stores**: seven DynamoDB tables (builds, counters, proposals, the agent's conversations and messages, realtime connections, the gallery audit trail) and seven S3 buckets (site, gallery files, agent snapshots, config, and three log buckets).
- **Secrets**: two Secrets Manager secrets, both generated at deploy: the invite code, and the key the Realtime block signs channel tokens with.
- **Scheduled job**: an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that runs the same function once a minute to pick the build of the hour and write the gallery snapshot through the custom Block, HouseBucket.
- **Observability**: a Logger, Metrics, a CloudWatch dashboard, three alarms and one SNS topic.
- **Identity**: one IAM role shared by the API function, the scheduled job and the AgentCore runtime.

### What the deployer chooses

`BASEPLATE_TAGS`, `BASEPLATE_RETAIN_DATA`, `BASEPLATE_API_WAF` and `BASEPLATE_ALARM_EMAIL`, read from the environment at deploy.

dataflow.description:
### Data flows

1. A visitor's browser loads the page from CloudFront over HTTPS. An invite link carries the code in the URL fragment; the page keeps it in sessionStorage.
2. The page calls open API methods to read the gallery and to check in every 15 seconds with a random session id.
3. The page opens a WebSocket with a channel token from `joinGallery` and receives gallery events. It can't publish.
4. With the invite code, the page saves a build (piece ids only). The function checks the code, takes budgets, writes the build and publishes an event.
5. With the invite code, the page asks the agent a question of at most 300 characters. The function checks the code, the conversation's owner and the budgets, then calls the model. The model answers through a tool limited to seven piece ids, and its reply text streams back on the conversation's channel.
6. Once a minute the scheduled job reads recent builds and writes a snapshot file to the gallery bucket through the custom Block, with an audit entry.
7. The deployer's machine, or CI, installs packages from npm and synthesizes and deploys the stack with the AWS CDK.

### What's stored

- Saved builds: piece ids, a source, a time. No visitor text. No expiry.
- Agent conversations and messages: the visitor's questions and the model's answers. No expiry.
- Counters and presence markers: numbers under keys that hold a date, a minute or a random session id. They expire.
- The invite code, in Secrets Manager.
- Logs: reasons for refusals, build ids and pieces, question lengths. No question text and no addresses from the app's own logging.

### Trust boundaries and STRIDE

STRIDE is applied per element type: an external entity gets S and R, a process all six, a data store T, R, I and D, a data flow T, I and D.

| Boundary | Element type | STRIDE that applies | Threats | Not raised, and why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The visitor's browser and the static page from CloudFront | process | S, T, R, I, D, E | T8 (TI), T20 (TI), T21 (D) | S: The page has no sign-in to spoof; the invite code is covered under the invite boundary. R: The page stores nothing a visitor could later deny; refusals are logged on the server (threat 14). E: The page holds no privilege beyond the invite code (threat 8). |
| The internet and the REST API (API Gateway, one Lambda function) | process | S, T, R, I, D, E | T4 (D), T14 (R), T16 (TD), T23 (I) | S: Covered under the invite boundary (threats 1 to 3): the API itself has no authorizer. E: Covered under the account boundary (threat 12). |
| The internet and the WebSocket API (the Realtime block) | data flow | T, I, D | T9 (ST) | I: The gallery channel carries public data; agent channels need the invite and ownership (threat 10). D: Shares the stage throttle (threat 4). |
| Anonymous callers and invite holders, inside the handler | external entity | S, R | T1 (S), T2 (S), T3 (SR), T10 (I) | Nothing left out |
| The function and the model (the Agent block on Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Haiku 5.5) | process | S, T, R, I, D, E | T5 (D), T7 (TE) | S: The function calls the model with the stack's role; no caller identity reaches it. R: The Agent block stores each question and answer (threat 11). I: The model sees the question, the system prompt and the public catalog. Stored gallery content never reaches it. |
| The function and its stores (DynamoDB, S3, Secrets Manager) | data store | T, R, I, D | T6 (D), T11 (I), T13 (TI), T15 (R), T22 (D) | Nothing left out |
| The stack's one IAM role and the rest of the deployer's account | process | S, T, R, I, D, E | T12 (E) | S: The role is assumed by Lambda and by AgentCore in this account only, per its trust policy in the template. T: Covered by threat 12. R: CloudTrail is the deployer's account setting, outside this stack. I: Covered by threats 11 and 12. D: Covered by threats 4 and 5. |
| npm, GitHub and readers of the repository, and the deployer's machine and CI | external entity | S, R | T17 (TE), T18 (S), T19 (I) | R: Commits and releases are the repository host's record; the sample adds nothing. |

assumptions.content: A person who clones the repository deploys the stack into an AWS account they control. AWS hosts no running copy of this sample.
The deployer controls who can read the account's tables, logs, buckets and secret, and treats the deployment as a demo, not a production system.
The invite code is a shared demo code, not a sign-in. Anyone who has the link counts as invited.
The app collects no personal data by design. The one free-text field is the question to the agent.

The CDK Blocks packages behave as their pinned versions read on 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-27: aws-cdk-blocks 1.0.1 and @aws-cdk-blocks/core 1.0.1, and, under @aws-cdk-blocks, bb-agent, bb-realtime, bb-kv-store, bb-secret and hosting 1.0.0, which is still the latest release of each.

The branch ran on AWS in four test deploys by the maintainers on 2026-11-19 and 2026-11-20 on the earlier packages (@aws-blocks/blocks 0.9.0), and twice on CDK Blocks 1.0.0 on 2026-11-21, at the commit before the builder's data was read again: once deployed, used and destroyed, and once deployed and left running. All were in one account and one Region (us-east-1). A custom:observed entry that cites live-deploy/v1 is from 1.0.0; every other one is from the earlier release, and for those what 1.0.0 does when deployed comes from the code, the tests and the synthesized template. The CI workflow has never run.
Amazon Bedrock runs the model through a global inference profile, so a question may be processed in an AWS Region other than the stack's.

The deployer's account has access to Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock: Anthropic's use case details are submitted and the AWS Marketplace subscription is active. Until then the agent answers with an error and the rest of the app works. The maintainers' account already had access, so that first-call path wasn't seen.

threats.statement: An actor on the network path, or who finds a bucket or table exposed by a setting can read or change data in transit or at rest, which leads to disclosure or tampering of saved builds, questions, the snapshot or logs, negatively impacting the tables and the buckets

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. With the default CloudFront certificate the security policy is fixed at TLSv1, so the site accepts TLS 1.0 and later (cdk-nag CFR4); docs/security.md says so and the deploy prints a warning. Six buckets and the tables use keys AWS manages. Five buckets have no server access logging of their own; three of them are log buckets, and CloudFront logs requests for the site bucket.

threats.threatImpact: a deployer who can see that a flood or a refusal happened and can't see where it came from

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. API Gateway access logging is off, which is the CDK Blocks default; turning it on changes an account-wide API Gateway role. cdk-nag reports it (APIG1, APIG6). A refusal is now one WARN line with its reason; it still names no caller.

A residual risk to accept. The Block's source is generator output, so the fix (record first, then mark stored) belongs in the generator. The docs and the page no longer claim an entry for every write. The uploadedBy value is a label the app supplies, not an identity.

threats.prerequisites: who controls or exploits a package this repository installs
threats.threatAction: run code during install, build, synth or in the deployed function
threats.threatImpact: tampered output or use of the deployer's credentials and the stack's role
threats.statement: An actor who controls or exploits a package this repository installs can run code during install, build, synth or in the deployed function, which leads to tampered output or use of the deployer's credentials and the stack's role, negatively impacting the deployer's machine and account and the build

metadata.value: Medium

No advisory is ignored in the scanner settings. Version 4 listed one, minimatch 10.2.6 (CVE-2026-118764), bundled in aws-cdk-lib 2.277.0. aws-cdk-lib is now 2.278.0, whose bundled minimatch is 11.0.9, and the ignore entry is gone; npm audit reads 0 vulnerabilities. Three upgrades didn't wait out the 7-day cooldown that Dependabot applies: every CDK Blocks package moved to 1.0.0 on 2026-11-21, one day after those packages were published; aws-cdk-lib moved to 2.278.0 on 2026-11-22, two days after its release; and aws-cdk-blocks and @aws-cdk-blocks/core moved to 1.0.1 on 2026-11-27, four days after their release. In @aws-cdk-blocks/core the only published runtime file that differs between 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 is the version string, and aws-cdk-blocks 1.0.1 adds a command line entry point that this sample doesn't call. The CDK Blocks packages come from the aws/cdk-blocks repository under the names aws-cdk-blocks and @aws-cdk-blocks. Two direct dependencies were new in version 2: @aws-sdk/client-s3 3.1172.0, which the tree already held, and playwright 1.65.1 for the contrast test. The lockfile marks playwright devOptional, because bedrock-agentcore names it as an optional peer; the bundles a deploy uploads hold none of it. CI downloads a Chromium build with Playwright's installer. The CI workflow has never run.

threats.threatImpact: a reader who copies the import into another project and runs npm install on that name getting the actor's code
threats.statement: An actor who registers the @your-team scope on the public npm registry can publish a package named @your-team/bb-house-bucket, which leads to a reader who copies the import into another project and runs npm install on that name getting the actor's code, negatively impacting a reader's own project

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. This repository's own install can't reach the registry for that name. The exposure left is a reader who copies the import name elsewhere; the page's download comment tells readers to copy the folder.

threats.prerequisites: who can read the repository, a shared invite link, a browser history or the logs
threats.threatAction: find the invite code or a deployer's identifiers there
threats.threatImpact: use of the save and ask methods by someone the deployer didn't invite
threats.statement: A person who can read the repository, a shared invite link, a browser history or the logs can find the invite code or a deployer's identifiers there, which leads to use of the save and ask methods by someone the deployer didn't invite, negatively impacting the invite code

metadata.value: Medium

A deployer can still paste the code into a place that keeps it. A forwarded link carries the code to whoever receives it; see threat 3. The secrets scan of the working tree reads the files git tracks or would track, so a secret in a folder .gitignore names isn't scanned; such a file can't be committed.

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. There's no Content-Security-Policy header, which is the Hosting construct's default. The page has no HTML sink and the API has no cookie, so the header would be a second layer.

threats.prerequisites: with a weak or unusual GPU path
threats.threatAction: keep drawing the scene while idle, or fail to start the renderer after a graphics adapter was found
threats.threatImpact: battery use on the visitor's device, or a blank stage
threats.statement: A visitor's own browser or device with a weak or unusual GPU path can keep drawing the scene while idle, or fail to start the renderer after a graphics adapter was found, which leads to battery use on the visitor's device, or a blank stage, negatively impacting the page on that device

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. The render loop runs always unless reduced motion is on; changing it alters every animation. A rejected renderer start after an adapter was found may leave the stage blank; that's inferred, and no browser on hand fails that way.

threats.prerequisites: that replaces the invite secret while a copy of the function is running
threats.threatAction: leave that copy holding the old secret's address
threats.threatImpact: save and ask calls that fail at random until that copy retires
threats.statement: A deploy that replaces the invite secret while a copy of the function is running can leave that copy holding the old secret's address, which leads to save and ask calls that fail at random until that copy retires, negatively impacting the save and agent methods

metadata.value: Low

Covers the invite secret only. A Block that reads its address when the module loads, such as a table or a bucket, stays stale if a deploy replaces it; docs/deploy.md gives the restart command. The retry has run in tests only. The cause is in CDK Blocks' config loading and needs an upstream issue. The failure is closed: a copy that can't read the code refuses.

threats.prerequisites: who has the site or API address
threats.threatAction: request /cdk-blocks/dashboard, /cdk-blocks/resources or /cdk-blocks/settings and read where the redirect points
threats.threatImpact: the AWS Region and the stack's name, which holds the stack id, known to a stranger
threats.statement: An internet actor who has the site or API address can request /cdk-blocks/dashboard, /cdk-blocks/resources or /cdk-blocks/settings and read where the redirect points, which leads to the AWS Region and the stack's name, which holds the stack id, known to a stranger, negatively impacting the deployment's identifiers

metadata.value: Low

A residual risk to accept. The app keeps the stack name out of its own API, and these routes give it away. It isn't a credential: the console pages need the deployer's sign-in, and no account id is in the address. Removing the routes needs an option in CDK Blocks, or a rule in front of the API that the sample doesn't add. Read in the library and the template. On 2026-11-21 the maintainers requested /cdk-blocks/dashboard on the 1.0.0 stack and it answered 302 to the console, with the Region and the stack name in the address; the other two routes weren't requested.
